items.reason: Nxd4 trades knight for bishop; after Nxd4 Re8+ Be2, Qxb6 regains the pawn with equality.
Rg8 attacks the queen; after 2.Qh6, Ng3 forks the h1 rook, matching the engine line.
h6 does attack the g5 knight, but it doesn't open the h-file. The move also allows exf6, losing material.
a4 hits b5, opens queenside files, undoes Black's majority and frees Nc3's squares; Ne4 was stronger.
h6 opens no file; it simply attacks the g5 bishop. Engine prefers e6.
Nxd7 wins the queen, and the d7 knight attacks e5; White defends with f4.
Bg3 does save the attacked bishop, but there is no tempo and no trade that traps the queen.
Castling gets the king out of the centre to a full pawn shield and brings the rook toward c1.
Even knight trade gives no extra piece; Black is a pawn down, and the real point is ...Bxf5.
Nf8 does defend the king, but it doesn't attack f4. Only a later Ng6 would. h3 was better.
Black's queen is on g3, not the d-file. The real point, cxd4 Bb4 hitting the queen, is missed.
Bxe4 dxe4 leaves no extra piece and hits the f3 rook. Nxc4, regaining the pawn, was best.
exd5 is a capture, not a recapture, but it does remove the d5 pawn attacking the c6 knight.
Bxb3 does hit Rd1, but axb3 just recaptures; the idea ignores the knight on g4, attacked by h3.
Nxe5 regains the pawn, but the knight itself hits the queen; no queen-on-queen follow-up exists.
No extra piece: after Nxe4 dxe4 Qxe4 White only nets a pawn. Castling is part of the plan.
Ne7 defends the pinned c6 knight, but it gains no tempo. Bd7 would also keep the bishop pair.
After Bxd4 no rook can usefully hit the bishop; the engine follow-up is ...c5, a pawn attack.
Nf3 attacks no bishop, and White has only one bishop, so there is no bishop pair.
A knight on d4 neither guards c3 nor attacks the rooks on c8/f7. Bc2 was best.
Nd7 does attack c5, but it doesn't hit White's queen on d1; the real point is recapturing a piece.
Winning the g3 bishop is correct, but e4 doesn't restrain White's queenside pawns and falls to Nxe4 anyway.
Bg5 pins nothing, and after hxg4 material is level, so there is no extra piece. Nd4 wins.
axb3 wins the knight on b3, which attacked the queen on d2; this is the engine's best move.
White's king on d1 has no castling rights, so 'castle' is impossible. Bxb4 also gives up the bishop for no clear gain.
Bh7+ gains no time; king simply steps aside and the bishop ends up offside. e5 was already capturable.
The b2 pawn doesn't attack the queen. c5 holds Black's own pawn, not a White knight.
From f5 the knight attacks no rook. The e7 knight was already defended by the king, so there is no tempo.
Bb4 develops and attacks the c3 queen with tempo; the king's pawn shield stays intact, as in the engine line.
Qg6+ forces no queen trade. After Ng5, Black wins the pinned knight, not a bishop.
Nf3 doesn't attack b7. Its real point is blocking the long diagonal, shielding the h1 rook.
h6 does attack the g5 bishop, but it does not open the h-file; no pawns get exchanged there.
Ne8 saves the attacked knight and opens the g7 bishop, so Nd7 and Bg7 now pressure e5.
h4 can't become passed: White's h2 and g3 pawns block it. Also Nxh4 recaptures without wrecking the kingside.
c1 holds a bishop, not a knight; cxd4 captures the d4 pawn rather than attacking it.
King safety is a real reason to castle, but castling does nothing for the c8 bishop, still blocked by e6/d7.
The d5 pawn attacks e6 and c6, not Black's king or bishop. exd5 is right because it recovers material.
A knight on c3 does not attack d6 and does not guard the king. Nc3 is also worse than Qd3.
After exd4 White's own d4 pawn blocks the b2–e5 diagonal, so the bishop is shut in rather than active.
Qd3 does defend the doubly attacked c3 knight. It misses the bigger point, the Qh7# threat, and Qh5 is stronger.
Ng5 saves the knight and hits e4, but Bg5 is impossible with the knight there. It misses the real f7/Qh5 attack.
Nxg4 captures the queen for a decisive material gain. The rook remark is accurate but adds little.
d5 doesn't attack the d7 queen or open the d-file. It misses the stronger Nxb5.
The queen already hits d5 and a8, so gxf3 adds nothing; it only weakens White's king.
e4 does hit the f3 knight, but the c8 bishop was already free since d7 is empty.
Ne5 saves the hanging c4 knight, but it attacks neither the f4 queen nor the h3 bishop, so there's no tempo.
Rxc1 grabs a bishop but ignores Qf6+ Kh7 Qg6+ Kh8 Qg8#; Rxg2+ was needed.
Qxa2 saves the queen and wins a pawn, but from a2 the queen does not attack the c1 rook.
Qxb4 saves the queen and wins a pawn, but gains no tempo; White's Rb1 hits the queen instead.
The c-file is open, and Rc6 or Rd8 can attack d6. Winning d6 is the position's key theme.
The a2 rook is undefended, so Bxa2 wins it outright. The bishop on a2 is also currently undefended.
e4 does attack the rook, but it doesn't open the e-file. It also misses the forced mate starting with Qg7+.
Bb3 does not guard the king; it mainly sidesteps the Rd8 pressure. "Keep the queen" is vague and irrelevant.
Nf4 rescues the knight from h5xg6 and attacks the undefended h5 pawn, also eyeing d5 and g2.
e5 is undefended, so Qxe5 escapes the g6 attack and wins a pawn. Qc8 wins much more.
Bg4 isn't attacked (Nf5 hits d4), and the trade leaves material equal with no extra piece and no pawn ending.
Nh6 attacks no rook; it saves the knight passively, while Nxe5 wins a pawn and is better.
Capturing the knight is correct, but the c4 bishop doesn't guard h2, and the knight's gone anyway.
f6 does attack the g5 bishop, but the f-file stays closed because the pawn still sits on f6.
White is in check, so Re1 is a block, not tempo. Black simply plays Rxe1+, winning the rook.
A rook on d8 attacks neither the e7 rook nor the king; Rfe8 would contest e7.
Castling ignores that the d5 queen is attacked by Bb7; Bxd5 wins it. Retreating the queen comes first.
Ng7+ gains no time: Kxg7 wins the undefended knight. It also misses the immediate mate Be2#.
The open file is g, not f; Kf8 steps onto f. The e7 rook is on Black's second rank, not seventh.
Rc1 checks the king, not the queen; the e2 bishop guards nothing and falls to Nxe2+.
Rb7 puts the rook next to Black's queen on b8, and nothing defends it. Qxb7 simply wins the rook.
cxb5 opens the c-file: Qxc2 Rxc2 Rxc2 drops a rook. White never gets an extra pawn.
Rxd5 wins the bishop and the rook then hits e5, which it later captures in the engine line.
Nd2 does fork the queen on b3 and the rook on f1; this is the engine's best move.
e4 does not open the f-file and creates no mating net; Nxf7 is far stronger.
The bishop is already developed and the queen isn't threatened; Bxf6+ is a pawn capture opening Black's king.
Nxb5 rescues the attacked d4-knight and wins the bishop. The e7 rook stays hit by Bd6, so White must move it.
Rg8 saves the attacked rook and hits Bg7; the main line later trades bishops with Bxc3.
Rb8 neither guards the d8 king nor affects e5, which isn't attacked. It misses 1...e6 trapping the f7 bishop.
The queen on d8 wasn't attacked, so nothing needed saving. But Qd4 does hit the undefended e3 queen with tempo.
Black is in check from Bc6; the e-file isn't open. Kd8 escapes check but also weakens the king's shelter.
Rg3+ is check, but Qxg3 simply wins the rook, so it neither gains time nor harasses the queen.
Qe5+ does trade queens, but then Black has no queen left to guard a7; the rook defends instead.
Rb8 doesn't attack c4 or add king safety; it seizes the open b-file to double on the second rank.
a5 attacks b4, not either rook. It ignores the pinned c6-knight; Rxc6 wins a piece.
Ne3 really forks both rooks on d5 and d1, which is a genuine tactical reason. Engine prefers Kh8.
Re1 does check Ke7 along the open e-file; Nxe1 removes the checker and wins the exchange.
Kg7 adds a defender to f6, but Qd6 still wins c6 or a6, so pawns aren't kept intact.
The bishop on g4 is attacked, but Be6 lets White play Bxe6 with gain, unlike the stronger Nxd5.
Correct: Qxf5 allows Qxg7 mate, so Rxf5 keeps g7 guarded. But exf5 also does that, and scores better.
c1 rook is undefended; Rxc1 wins it back, restores material balance, and parries Rxe1+.
d4 doesn't attack White's king and ignores the Rxh7# threat; Black gets mated immediately.
Nxa1+ wins rook with check (Ka4 forced), but no king-bishop fork follows; ignores Bxb8 threat.
A king cannot block a diagonal. Kh1 leaves the king exposed to Bf4+ and Be3+; Kf2 holds much better.
Rg3 stays on the g-file and never touches the b-file. It only eyes g6, while White's king stays exposed.
g3 does attack the f4 knight, but pushing it to g3 does not open the g-file.
Qh5 does not check the king on g7. It only defends e5 along the rank and pins nothing.
Rooks have no diagonals, and the queen on a7 cannot block on e1/f1. White simply plays Kg2.
bxc6 removes the knight attacking b8 and opens the b-file, where the rook now hits b5.
Nothing defends d6: c6 blocks the queen. Bxd6 wins a whole bishop, as the engine's best line shows.
Rg8+ creates no escape square for White's king, and g5 is defended by f6 and the queen, so it can't simply be grabbed.
f6 does attack the g5 bishop, but advancing it does not open the f-file.
Bishops move diagonally and cannot use a file. Rxd8 also passes up the winning 1.c4.
Bc4 covers e2/f1 and eyes d5, but b3 already hit d5; ignores hanging h3. Bxd5 best.
Rooks have no diagonal, and Kf7 blocks nothing. It unpins the e7 bishop while attacking the e6 rook.
